imageCaption: A handwritten index card sits on the Gomez family's kitchen counter, surrounded by post-it notes and hastily scrawled addresses. The card reads: 'Monthly Sunday Supper — You're invited to keep cooking.' In the background, barely visible, is one edge of Anthony's license plate pegboard.
text:
The invitation arrived as a glitch.

Not one of the big ones—not the kind that split kitchens in half or rewrote the past tense—but the small kind that Aaliyah was learning to recognize as the timeline showing off. The kind that made the world seem momentarily friendlier, like it was winking at you.

She was standing outside Marco's colmadón waiting for Elijah to stop talking to a pigeon about snack distribution when the mailbox decided to exist in two states at once.

One version was empty.

The other version was absolutely full.

Aaliyah watched the temporal glitch for exactly three seconds before reaching in. Her hand moved through both states—the empty one and the full one—like she was reaching through two possibilities at the same time. She pulled out a single index card. The glitch collapsed. The mailbox was empty again. The card was completely real.

*We would like you to cook again,* it read in careful handwriting that looked like it had been written by at least four different people. *Monthly, on Sundays. The neighborhood has decided. Please bring chaos.*

The back had addresses. Fourteen of them. Thirteen houses and Marco's colmadón. A map of people who'd tasted mofongo blessed by time itself and decided that the Gomez family wasn't allowed to leave.

"What'd you get?" Elijah asked, abandoning the pigeon with the commitment of someone who'd found a better friend approximately forty seconds ago.

"We're being conscripted into community service," Aaliyah said, reading the list. "By very polite people who've apparently organized."

"That's the best kind of conscription," Elijah decided. He looked at the card like it was a treasure map. "Are we still going to Curaçao?"

"Yeah," Aaliyah said. "We're still going. This just means... I don't know. The neighborhood gets a vote in when."

They walked home with the card held carefully between them, like it was something that might disappear if they weren't paying attention. The afternoon was bright in that specific way of summer New York mornings that had decided to be generous—everything gold-edged, everything possible.

When they got to the yellow house, their parents were both in the living room, which was unusual. Anthony was holding the license plate pegboard like he was seeing it for the first time. Luisana was on her phone, speaking rapidly in Spanish to someone who was apparently very invested in property speculation.

"Your mother has been on the phone with a real estate agent in Willemstad for seventeen minutes," Anthony said by way of greeting. "She started speaking so fast I can only catch every third word, but I'm fairly certain she's describing the kitchen in our theoretical future house like she's already lived in it."

"Because I have lived in it," Luisana said, covering the phone. "In emails. In late-night listings. In every version of this journey where we knew where we were going. The agent is very confused because I'm asking extremely specific questions about water pressure and whether the kitchen window gets afternoon light, which is apparently what a person who is definitely buying a house sounds like."

"Look what came," Aaliyah said, holding out the card.

Luisana took it from the phone conversation—"Perdón, uno momento"—and read it three times. Her expression moved through surprise, understanding, and then something that looked like she was holding her own heart and realizing it had grown larger without asking permission.

"They want us to stay," she said quietly.

"They want us to cook," Aaliyah corrected. "They want chaos on Sundays. They're very specific about the chaos."

Anthony took the card next. He read the addresses—fourteen neighborhoods, fourteen people, fourteen versions of the choice to belong. And something shifted in his face. Aaliyah recognized it because she'd seen it happen every time he'd had to move before she was born, every time his family had decided a place wasn't big enough to hold his enthusiasm.

It was the look of a person realizing that someone had built a container just exactly his size.

"So we can't leave until we've cooked fourteen times?" he said.

"Unless we're very rude to the entire neighborhood," Aaliyah said. "Which seems unlikely. Marco taught you manners."

"Marco taught me a lot of things," Anthony said. He was still holding the pegboard. The blank plate that wasn't-Barbados was still there, still impossible, still pointing toward Curaçao. "He taught me that spontaneity only works if you're spontaneous with the right people. And apparently, we've found the right people."

Elijah appeared in the doorway with Sully, who barked once in agreement. The bark of a dog who understood that some invitations were decisions, and some decisions were the entire point.

"This means we stay for at least four months," Luisana said, doing the math. "Monthly Sundays. Four rounds of chaos before the next plate becomes real enough to follow."

"Maybe longer," Aaliyah said. She was thinking about the glitch in the mailbox. The way the timeline had delivered the invitation so carefully. Like it was making sure they understood that belonging to a place and leaving a place weren't opposites. They were just different speeds of the same movement. "Maybe we stay until the fourteenth Sunday. Maybe they make us. Maybe we want to."

"Can we cook something different each time?" Elijah asked, which was the important question. The one that meant he understood this wasn't about repetition. It was about showing a neighborhood exactly who his family was, one recipe at a time.

"Completely different," Aaliyah confirmed. "Every Sunday we prove we're weird in seventeen new ways."

Sully barked again. Three short barks this time. And then he walked over to the window and stared out at the street like he was already seeing it the way they'd see it four months from now—familiar enough to be home, chaotic enough to be honest.

"Okay," Anthony said. He put the pegboard down very gently on the coffee table, next to Luisana's journal, like he was placing a map where the whole family could see it. "So we have four months. Four Sundays. Four chances to give the neighborhood exactly what they're asking for."

"Which is?" Luisana asked, though she already knew.

"All of us," Anthony said. "Everything we are. No planning."

And Aaliyah understood, sitting in the yellow house with her family gathered around the pegboard and the invitation and the impossible plate that knew exactly where home was—understood that this wasn't a detour.

This was the moment the journey became real.

Because now they weren't just traveling through places where broken time needed fixing.

Now they were building the kind of place that people wanted them to stay.

And that changed everything.
